blocks.content: If the direct and associative effects are uncorrelated, this reduces to the standard result that the covariance between an individual's phenotype and breeding value is simply the additive genetic variance (in this case, of direct effects). By contrast, the variance of the total breeding value becomes [[SEE_FORMULA:22.4c]]

Equation 22.4d shows that the covariance between total breeding value and phenotype is different from the variance in total breeding value. This reflects the fact that the associative effects of an individual do not influence its own phenotype. Note from Equation 22.4c that $ \sigma(A_{d}, A_{s}) $ and $ \sigma^{2}(A_{s}) $ are scaled by $ (n-1) $ and $ (n-1)^{2} $ , respectively, in $ \sigma^{2}(A_{T}) $ . Hence, with even modest group sizes, small values of $ \sigma(A_{d}, A_{s}) $ and $ \sigma^{2}(A_{s}) $ can still have a very significant impact. Some of the early papers reporting estimates of these two quantities ignored this scaling with n, and hence tended to downplay the importance of social interactions (Chen et al. 2006; Van Vleck et al. 2007).

If we assume (for now) that the group members are unrelated, then $ (P_ d_i, P_ s_j) = 0 $. For a group of size $ n $, Equation 22.5a reduces to [[SEE_FORMULA:22.5b]] [[SEE_FORMULA:22.5c]] [[SEE_FORMULA:22.5d]] where $ e $ is given by Equation 22.1c. With the phenotypic variance in hand, we can define the heritability of the direct and associative effects, $ h_d^2 $ and $ h_s^2 $, respectively, as [[SEE_FORMULA:22.6a]]

The careful reader will note that there is a different, but perhaps more natural, definition of these two heritabilities. Equation 22.6a standardizes the genetic variances with respect to the total trait variance, but one could also standardize them with respect to the variance of direct and associative effects, for example, [[SEE_FORMULA:22.6b]]

We use a prime to distinguish these from the hertiabilities scaled to total trait variance $ \left( \sigma^{2}\left(P_{x}\right)\right) $ vs. $ \sigma_{z}^{2} $ . While heritabilities scaled by $ \sigma_{z}^{2} $ (Equation 22.6a) are the most widespread in the literature, there are some advantages to scaling heritabilities by $ \sigma^{2}\left(P_{x}\right) $ (where $ x=d $ or s). On this scale, the heritabilities measure the fraction of additive genetic variation in the actual effect (direct or associative) itself, rather than in the trait value. Further, $ h_{x^{\prime}}^{2} $ is independent of the group size (provided that $ A_{s} $ does not change with group size), as $ \sigma^{2}\left(P_{x}\right) $ is independent of n, while $ \sigma_{z}^{2} $ is a function of n (Equation 22.5b).

In keeping with Equation 22.6a, we can similarly define the “heritability” of the total breeding value as [[SEE_FORMULA:22.7a]] as suggested by Bijma et al. (2007a). The reason we have used $ T^2 $ rather than $ h_T^2 $ is that, unlike heritabilities, $ T^2 $ can exceed one. This can happen because $ ^2(A_T) $ contains additional terms not found in $ _z^2 $, as the associative effect of an individual influences others in the group, rather than the individual in which it resides.
